newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russia declines NATO offer to exchange officers.
newsitem.headline: Russia declines NATO offer to exchange officers.

text.p: Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov warned the West on Wednesday that plans to expand NATO into former communist Eastern Europe would jeopardise arms control.

Declining a NATO offer to exchange military liasion officers, Rodionov told his NATO counterparts the alliance's planned enlargement would upset the balance of power in Europe and leave Moscow no option but to take counter-measures.
"We cannot rule out that NATO enlargement will stall implementation of certain (arms control) treaties and make it more difficult to conclude new ones," he said.
He said Moscow would adopt political, military, and economic measures in response, but declined to specify what they might be.
"The position is as follows: NATO enlargement to the east is unacceptable to Russia," Rodionov told a joint news conference with the 16-nation alliance's Secretary General Javier Solana.
"We don't understand why other countries are being taken on board and Russia is being ignored," he said, warning exclusion could mean "a return to the bad-old-days" of East-West rivalry.
Rodoniov, dressed in sombre grey suit, left the military this week to become modern Russia's first civilian defence minister.
He surprised NATO ministers with one of the most forthright denunciations of enlargement in recent months, employing language more akin to the days of the Cold War.
"Many ministers were disappointed by the language of the past... the Cold War is over but the debate is loaded with Cold War legacies," said one official.
The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) had hoped Rodionov would agree to an exchange of military liasion officers to build on recent cooperation in an alliance-led peace force in Bosnia.
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said Last week Moscow was ready to open talks on a radical new relationship, embodied in a charter or treaty, despite the differences over enlargement.
NATO officials were quick to play down Rodionov's negative comments, saying Primakov was the man in charge and Solana would begin talks qith him in Moscow in late January.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, attending his last NATO meeting, emphasised the common ground that now existed between the former enemies.
"We stand shoulder-to-shoulder in Bosnia, we made great progress in arms control and military cooperation," he told reporters.

NATO is adamant it will move ahead with enlargement at a July 8-9 summit in Madrid next year when it will invite some countries to open accession talks. But it wants the same summit to endorse the new deal with Russia.

NATO defence ministers also agreed on Wednesday to bolster the so-called Partnership of Peace programme with Eastern Europe, in which they take part in peacekeeping missions, to console those who will not join NATO in the first wave.
"The partnership for peace continues to play a dynamic and important role in the development of a new security architecture," the ministers said in a statement.

Ties between the former foes have been boosted by Russian participation and help in planning a Stabilisation Force to Bosnia aimed at ensuring the country does not slip back into war after December 20 when the mandate of the current force expires.
